doc.title: John Altman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 14, 2023

title: Writing for orchestras of varying line-ups
summary: He writes to the available players, from a community orchestra to the LSO and Royal Philharmonic.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah I was envious of one of the many videos had you standing in front of a huge orchestra and is there a difference for you — you said when I book an orchestra, which I’m assuming you’re booking only the instrumentalists that you want, that you wrote for. So if you get a commission to write for a full orchestra have you ever had the issue of there’s more instruments here than I really need but I better write something for the second bassoon because they’ve been sitting there for a long time?

I know what you mean. No, it never really comes up, you know because if you’re given the orchestral resource, I mean for example I wrote something for a community orchestra in the Midlands, and they said well we’ve got like 18 flute players or something like that, and one violin. So what you write is actually based on what their line-up is. And it’s interesting because it then becomes a challenge. You think what am I doing to do with all these people? How am I going to — and the ones who can’t actually play as well as the other ones, do I write the same things for them? So there are different challenges. But I’ve been so lucky because when I write for orchestra if it’s not my own selection of players I’ve written for the LSO and for the Royal Philharmonic and the London Philharmonic and the Philharmonia and the Birmingham Symphony. So I know what I’m going to get you know. I know that whatever I write will be played exactly as I’ve written it. I’m not going to have to go in and say, “Hang on a minute, this is all wrong.”
